profile.summary: The Jores plant promoter CNN is a pair of convolutional neural networks that predict how strongly a plant core promoter drives gene expression. Each model takes a 170-base promoter sequence (from 165 bases upstream to 5 bases downstream of the transcription start site) and outputs a single number, the promoter strength measured by STARR-seq. One model was trained on measurements in tobacco leaves and the other on maize protoplasts, using promoters from Arabidopsis, maize and sorghum.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The sequence is one-hot encoded and passed to two forward- and reverse-strand scan layers, adapted from DeepGMAP, with 128 filters of width 13. These feed a standard convolutional layer (128 filters, width 13, ReLU). Each convolutional layer is followed by dropout at rate 0.15. A dense layer of 64 units with batch normalisation and ReLU leads to a final dense layer with one output. The first convolutional kernel is initialised with clustered transcription factor and core promoter element motifs. The models are trained as regressions with mean squared error loss on the measured enrichment, with Adam, early stopping and learning-rate reduction.

sections.title: Use for promoter design
sections.body: The authors used the models for in silico evolution. In each round, every single-nucleotide variant of a promoter is scored and the best is kept for the next round. Scoring can use the tobacco model, the maize model, or the mean of both. The authors synthesised and tested promoters after three and ten rounds. They report a large rise in measured strength after three rounds and a smaller further rise after ten, and that the averaged score gave promoters active in both systems.

profile.summary: Orthrus is a family of RNA foundation models that turn a full mature mRNA transcript into an embedding. It was pretrained so that splice isoforms of the same gene, and transcripts of orthologous genes across mammals, get similar embeddings. The embeddings are used, directly or after fine-tuning, to predict mRNA properties such as RNA half-life and ribosome load.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Orthrus uses a Mamba encoder, a state-space model whose memory grows linearly with sequence length, so it can read whole mRNAs. The input is a per-base track matrix: four one-hot nucleotide tracks, plus in the 6-track models a coding sequence track (1 at the first base of each codon) and a splice track (1 at the last base of each exon). Pretraining is contrastive: the model maximises embedding similarity between pairs of transcripts formed from splice isoforms and orthologues. One released checkpoint adds a masked language modelling objective. The model returns a mean-pooled embedding per transcript, or per-position hidden states.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "antichronology/orthrus-4-track",
    trust_remote_code=True,
).to(device).eval()

sequence = (
    "TCATCTGGATTATACATATTTCGCAATGAAAGAGAGGAAGAAAAGGAAGCAGCAAAATATGTGGAGGCCCA"
    "ACAAAAGAGACTAGAAGCCTTATTCACTAAAATTCAGGAGGAATTTGAAGAACATGAAGTTACTTCCTCC"
)
oh = model.seq_to_oh(sequence).unsqueeze(0).to(device)  # (1, L, 4)
lengths = torch.tensor([oh.shape[1]], device=device)

with torch.no_grad():
    emb = model.representation(oh, lengths, channel_last=True)
# emb.shape == (1, D)
PY

profile.summary: RNAGenesis is an RNA foundation model that handles sequence representation, structure prediction and sequence design in one framework. A BERT-style encoder, pretrained with masked RNA modelling on non-coding RNAs, turns an RNA sequence into embeddings; a query-based compression step maps those into a short latent code, and a diffusion model generates new latent codes that a decoder turns back into sequences. It is used both to score or classify RNAs after fine-tuning and to design new ones, such as aptamers and CRISPR sgRNA scaffolds.
profile.summary_source_locator: Preprint abstract; README: Overview, Encoder Checkpoint for Embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The repository's pretraining configuration for the stage-one encoder uses single-nucleotide embeddings of width 1,280, six parallel convolutional layers with kernels 3 to 13 whose outputs are summed with those embeddings, and 32 bidirectional Transformer blocks with 20 attention heads, RoPE and SwiGLU feed-forward layers. Training is masked RNA modelling: 30% of positions are selected and the loss is cross-entropy on those positions only. The repository notes that masking happens before the convolutional embeddings, so the masked bases cannot leak through the convolutions. No source read says which configuration the released Zenodo and Hugging Face weights use. The repository tree also holds two files whose names contain 6layers_16heads_128embedsize. For generation, the encoder output is compressed into a latent code, a diffusion model samples new latent codes, and a decoder produces sequences. Sampling can be steered at inference time by a classifier gradient or by beam search.
sections.source_locator: PRETRAIN.md: Architecture and objective; preprint abstract; README: Inference Pipeline; repository tree: models/autoencoder/encoder/checkpoints/Pretrained

sections.title: What it is used for
sections.body: Two routes are documented. For understanding tasks, the pretrained encoder is fine-tuned: the repository's example adds LoRA adapters, averages the valid nucleotide embeddings and trains an MLP head for 13 ncRNA classes. For design, generation.py samples sequences from a diffusion checkpoint, with aptamer and sgRNA checkpoints given as examples, optionally with classifier guidance or beam search. A separate module fine-tunes the encoder for 3D structure prediction.

profile.summary: TREDNet predicts whether a 2,000 base pair stretch of human DNA acts as an enhancer, and how much a single-nucleotide variant changes that prediction. It works in two stages: a first convolutional network turns the one-hot encoded sequence into 1,924 predicted epigenomic signals (DNase I hypersensitivity, histone modifications and transcription factor binding), and a second, smaller network turns that vector into an enhancer probability for one tissue or cell line. Released phase two models cover pancreatic islets, HepG2 and K562.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Phase one is a multitask convolutional classifier in the style of DeepSEA, Beluga and DanQ. It takes a one-hot encoded 2,000 base window and outputs 1,924 values, one per epigenomic feature. Phase two is a smaller convolutional network trained on enhancer regions, but each region is first passed through phase one and so is represented by the 1,924-value vector rather than by its sequence. Phase two can be a single-output classifier for one tissue or a multitask classifier over several. Chromosomes 8 and 9 were held out of training and used for testing.
sections.source_locator: README: Phase one, Phase two; paper: Results; Kipoi model.yaml files: schema, info

sections.title: Scoring variants and regions
sections.body: The repository's score_variant.py reads a VCF, needs an hg19 FASTA, and writes a tab-separated file. With -score-iep it builds the 2,000 base reference and alternate sequences centred on the SNP, predicts both, and scores the variant as the larger probability times the absolute difference between the two. With -score-delta it takes the 2,000 base window around the variant, substitutes every other base at each position from 990 to 1010, averages the drop from the reference prediction at each position and divides by the median absolute value, writing the resulting list of values. Separately, the paper reports saturated mutagenesis across whole enhancers, which it calls enhancer damage (ED) scores, and defines peaks and dips in them as enhancer damaging regions (EDRs) and enhancer strengthening regions (ESRs). A second module, peak_detection/annotate.py, performs what the README calls PAS/DAS detection from a file of precomputed deltas.

profile.summary: DeepSTARR predicts how strongly a 249 base pair piece of DNA acts as an enhancer in Drosophila melanogaster S2 cells. It is a convolutional neural network with two outputs, one for developmental and one for housekeeping enhancer activity, trained on genome-wide UMI-STARR-seq measurements. Besides prediction, it is used to read out which nucleotides drive the predicted activity and so to study transcription factor motifs and their syntax.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The architecture is adapted from Basset: four convolutional layers, each followed by batch normalisation, a ReLU activation and max pooling, then two fully connected layers of 256 units and two single-unit output layers, Dense_Dev and Dense_Hk. The released model file gives 256 filters of width 7 in the first convolutional layer, then 60 of width 3, 60 of width 5 and 120 of width 3, with pooling size 2 throughout. The convolutional layers pick up local motifs and motif syntax; the fully connected layers combine them into one activity value per enhancer type. The model is a regression on measured UMI-STARR-seq activity, not a classifier.

sections.title: Interpreting the model
sections.body: The repository ships a second script that computes nucleotide contribution scores for a given sequence, separately for developmental or housekeeping activity, using DeepLIFT and SHAP. A Colab notebook runs the whole path end to end: training, contribution scores and TF-MoDISco motifs. The preprint states that the model learned TF motifs and higher-order syntax rules, including the effect of motif-flanking sequence and inter-motif distances, and that these rules were validated experimentally.

profile.summary: SpliceTransformer (SpTransformer) predicts RNA splicing from genomic sequence alone. For each position in a pre-mRNA sequence it gives the probability of being a splice donor, a splice acceptor or neither, and how much the site is used in each of 15 human tissues. Comparing predictions for reference and variant sequence lets it score how a genetic variant changes splicing in each tissue.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpTransformer has two main modules. An encoder of stacked convolutional residual blocks (ResBlocks) reads one-hot encoded sequence; the paper uses two such encoders with identical structure. Their output feeds a Sinkhorn Transformer, an attention variant built for long sequences, with 256 channels, 8 attention heads (two of them local) per layer and eight layers, followed by a multi-layer perceptron. For a 9000 nt input it predicts the central 1000 nt, using 4000 nt of context on each side. The output is an N x 3 matrix for splice site class and an N x 15 matrix for tissue usage. Training ran in two stages: first the two encoders were trained separately, one on GTEx data and one on an extra mammalian dataset, with 12 epochs per stage.

Its weights are too large for GitHub; Git-LFS access was disabled in November 2024, and the weights are now a single Google Drive download placed in model/weights. The download has no version label, so a result can only name the repository commit (this page read b67a51da) and the date the weights were fetched. The authors note that outputs can differ slightly between GPU types for individual variants. The variant annotation script uses a 95% threshold for tissue specificity unless raw scores are requested, so a result should say which output mode was used.

profile.summary: GenSLM (genome-scale language model) is a family of autoregressive language models that read DNA coding sequence as codons, three nucleotides per token. The foundation models were pretrained on over 110 million prokaryotic gene sequences, and a SARS-CoV-2 model was fine-tuned on 1.5 million viral genomes to track the virus's evolution and pick out variants of concern. The released code computes sequence embeddings and generates new sequences.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GenSLMs are generative pre-trained transformers (GPT-style causal language models) with a codon-level tokeniser. The released foundation models load GPT-NeoX architecture files (the 25M file declares GPTNeoXForCausalLM with 8 layers, hidden size 512 and 8 attention heads) and a 69-token codon vocabulary, and were trained at four sizes from 25 million to 25 billion parameters with a maximum sequence length of 2,048 tokens on individual genes from BV-BRC. The 25M and 250M models were then fine-tuned on SARS-CoV-2 genomes with sequence length 10,240 tokens; the larger sizes ran out of GPU memory at that length. The paper also describes a hierarchical model in which a diffusion model guides a codon-level transformer to cover whole genomes; the README points to a separate repository for it.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import numpy as np
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from genslm import GenSLM, SequenceDataset

model = GenSLM("genslm_25M_patric")
model.eval()
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model.to(device)

sequences = [
    "ATGAAAGTAACCGTTGTTGGAGCAGGTGCAGTTGGTGCAAGTTGCGCAGAATATATTGCA",
    "ATTAAAGATTTCGCATCTGAAGTTGTTTTGTTAGACATTAAAGAAGGTTATGCCGAAGGT",
]
dataset = SequenceDataset(sequences, model.seq_length, model.tokenizer)
dataloader = DataLoader(dataset)

embeddings = []
with torch.no_grad():
    for batch in dataloader:
        outputs = model(
            batch["input_ids"].to(device),
            batch["attention_mask"].to(device),
            output_hidden_states=True,
        )
        emb = outputs.hidden_states[-1].detach().cpu().numpy()
        emb = np.mean(emb, axis=1)
        embeddings.append(emb)

embeddings = np.concatenate(embeddings)
print(embeddings.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README embedding example wrapped in a shell heredoc. The model_cache_dir argument (a Colab Google Drive path in the README) is dropped so the default, the current directory, is used; comments are removed and the final bare expression is wrapped in print().

profile.summary: ESA-dna2vec is the DNA embedding model from the Embed-Search-Align (ESA) work, which treats read alignment as a search problem. A transformer encoder turns a DNA read or a reference genome fragment into a single vector, so that a read lands close to the fragment it came from. Reads are then aligned by searching a vector store of reference fragment embeddings and refining the best hits with Smith-Waterman scoring.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Figure 3 caption. Model card: Model Overview. GUANinE: list of evaluated models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model, called the Reference-Free DNA Embedding (RDE) model in the paper, is a transformer encoder with 12 heads, 6 encoder layers, a vocabulary of 10,000 tokens and 1020-dimensional output vectors. It is trained self-supervised with a contrastive loss: a read sampled from a reference fragment is pulled towards that fragment's embedding and pushed away from a batch of random fragments. The card describes fragments of 800 to 2000 bases, reads of 150 to 500 bases, and 1 to 5% random base substitutions added to 40% of training reads. For alignment, the reference genome is cut into overlapping fragments, each fragment is embedded and stored in a vector database, and each read retrieves its top-K nearest fragments per chromosome before Smith-Waterman scoring picks the best location.

    hf_model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("roychowdhuryresearch/dna2vec", trust_remote_code=True)
    hf_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("roychowdhuryresearch/dna2vec", trust_remote_code=True)

    class AveragePooler(nn.Module):
        def forward(self, last_hidden, attention_mask):
            return (last_hidden * attention_mask.unsqueeze(-1)).sum(1) / attention_mask.sum(-1).unsqueeze(-1)

    hf_model.pooler = AveragePooler()
    return hf_model, hf_tokenizer, hf_model.pooler

def get_embedding(dna_sequence):
    model, tokenizer, pooler = load_hf_model()
    tokenized_input = tokenizer(dna_sequence, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(**tokenized_input)
    embedding = pooler(output.last_hidden_state, tokenized_input.attention_mask)
    return embedding.numpy()

dna_seq = "ATGCGTACGTAGCTAGCTAGC"
embedding = get_embedding(dna_seq)
print("Embedding shape:", embedding.shape)

profile.summary: Carbon-X is a 14.8 billion parameter chat language model that reads DNA and English in the same conversation. You paste raw DNA into a message and ask a question; it answers in English, for example whether a mutation is likely benign or pathogenic, which organism group a sequence comes from, or what the next bases are. It was built from the general-purpose Qwen3-14B model by adding DNA tokens and further training on DNA and biology text.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNA and text share one token stream in one decoder, with no separate DNA encoder. A hybrid tokeniser keeps Qwen3's BPE vocabulary for text and encodes DNA as non-overlapping 6-mers, so one DNA token covers 6 base pairs; runs of at least 6 A, C, G or T bases are tagged as DNA automatically. Training had four stages. New DNA embeddings were first trained for about 10B tokens with the transformer frozen. The full model was then mid-trained on 302B tokens at sequence length 8,192, a mixture of 55% raw DNA, 20% English, 15% biology text and 10% instruction data. Supervised fine-tuning followed (3 epochs over 20 dataset subsets), then two rounds of GRPO reinforcement learning with code-checked rewards, all with thinking disabled.

profile.summary: LOL-EVE (Language Of Life for Evolutionary Variant Effects) scores the effect of insertions and deletions (indels) in human gene promoters without task-specific training. It is a conditional autoregressive transformer trained on 13.6 million mammalian promoter sequences, each tagged with its gene, species and clade. A variant is scored by comparing how likely the model finds the reference and the variant promoter sequence.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LOL-EVE is a causal language model based on the CTRL architecture, with 12 transformer layers, hidden size 768 and 12 attention heads. Each input starts with control codes for the gene, species and clade, followed by the promoter DNA between [SOS] and [EOS] tokens; training sequences were up to 1000 base pairs. The developers describe adaptive local position embeddings and say the model uses pretrained ESM protein embeddings for gene context. To score a variant, the reference and variant sequences are each run through the model with the same control codes, the summed cross-entropy of each is computed, and the score is the variant's minus the reference's, with higher meaning more deleterious.

python - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
import torch
import pandas as pd

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('Marks-lab/LOL-EVE')
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained('Marks-lab/LOL-EVE', trust_remote_code=True)

def score_variants_hf(variants_df, gene, species, clade):
    scores = []
    for _, row in variants_df.iterrows():
        ref_seq = f"{gene} {species} {clade} [SOS] {row['sequence']} [EOS]"
        var_seq = f"{gene} {species} {clade} [SOS] {row['variant_sequence']} [EOS]"
        ref_inputs = tokenizer(ref_seq, return_tensors="pt")
        var_inputs = tokenizer(var_seq, return_tensors="pt")
        with torch.no_grad():
            ref_outputs = model(**ref_inputs)
            var_outputs = model(**var_inputs)
            ref_logits = ref_outputs.logits[0, :-1]
            var_logits = var_outputs.logits[0, :-1]
            ref_tokens = ref_inputs['input_ids'][0, 1:]
            var_tokens = var_inputs['input_ids'][0, 1:]
            ref_score = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(ref_logits, ref_tokens, reduction='sum')
            var_score = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(var_logits, var_tokens, reduction='sum')
            score = (var_score - ref_score).item()
            scores.append(score)
    variants_df['score'] = scores
    return variants_df

variants = pd.DataFrame({
    'sequence': ['ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA', 'ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA'],
    'variant_sequence': ['ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA', 'ATGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTAGCTA']
})

scored_variants = score_variants_hf(variants, gene='brca1', species='human', clade='primate')
print(scored_variants)

profile.summary: PromoterAI is a deep learning model from Illumina that predicts how a variant in a gene promoter changes that gene's expression. It takes a list of variants (chromosome, position, reference and alternative allele, strand) and a reference genome, and adds a score between -1 and 1 to each variant: negative values mean lower expression and positive values mean higher expression. The authors built it to find noncoding promoter variants that may explain rare genetic diseases.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PromoterAI is a convolutional network written in TensorFlow and Keras. The code first projects one-hot DNA (4 channels) with a 1-wide convolution, then stacks blocks that each apply a dilated depthwise convolution and a two-layer dense step, with batch normalisation and residual connections. The README's training command uses 24 blocks of width 1024, a 20,480-base input and a 4,096-base output. The model is first trained to predict regulatory profiles stored as bigWig tracks around transcription start sites, optionally across several species, and is then fine-tuned on a GTEx variant file. For variant scoring, a twin wrapper runs the model on the reference and the alternative sequence and averages the difference between the two predictions.

profile.summary: hEvo is a family of DNA language models from MulinLab trained on haplotype sequences from human populations, so that the models see real human genetic variation rather than one reference genome. A model reads a DNA sequence of up to 1,024 nucleotides and returns one vector per nucleotide, plus masked-base predictions that can score a single-nucleotide variant as a log-likelihood ratio of the alternative against the reference allele. The authors use it for variant-effect scoring, regulatory annotation and population-genetic analysis.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hEvo is a bidirectional BERT-style masked language model with one token per nucleotide. Training has two stages. In Stage I the model learns representations by span masking on deduplicated haplotype windows drawn from population haplotypes. In Stage II the nucleotide prediction head is calibrated on contexts centred on variants. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant position is masked once and the log probability of the alternative allele minus that of the reference allele is taken from the same masked context; a positive value means the model prefers the alternative allele.

steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "MulinLab/hEVO-base-o"
# Freeze the checkpoint and its custom code for reproducible inference.
REVISION = "fa6139047c21d92b58bd8eda49ea2f89a884e33c"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

load_options = dict(revision=REVISION, token=True, trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO, **load_options)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    use_frequency_embedding=False,
    use_flash_attention=False,
    **load_options,
)
assert config.use_frequency_embedding is False
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    config=config,
    attn_implementation="eager",
    dtype=torch.float32,
    **load_options,
).to(device).eval()

def encode_dna(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.strip().upper()
    if not 0 < len(sequence) <= config.max_position_embeddings:
        raise ValueError("Provide a sequence of 1 to 1,024 nucleotides.")
    if set(sequence) - set("ACGTN"):
        raise ValueError("DNA must contain only A, C, G, T or N.")
    encoded = tokenizer(sequence, return_tensors="pt", truncation=False)
    # This custom tokenizer returns 1D tensors for a single sequence.
    encoded = {
        key: value.unsqueeze(0) if value.ndim == 1 else value
        for key, value in encoded.items()
    }
    if "attention_mask" not in encoded:
        encoded["attention_mask"] = torch.ones_like(encoded["input_ids"])
    return {key: value.to(device) for key, value in encoded.items()}

sequence = "ACGTTGCATGTCGCATGATGCATGAGAGCT"
inputs = encode_dna(sequence)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_dict=True)
    token_embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [batch, length, hidden_size]

    # Optional: summarize the last-layer nucleotide embeddings by mean pooling.
    keep = inputs["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).to(token_embeddings.dtype)
    sequence_embedding = (token_embeddings * keep).sum(dim=1) / keep.sum(
        dim=1
    ).clamp_min(1)

print("Last-layer token embeddings:", tuple(token_embeddings.shape))
print("Mean-pooled sequence embedding:", tuple(sequence_embedding.shape))
EOF
steps.explanation: The shared setup and the nucleotide embedding example from the hEVO-base-o card, joined and wrapped in a shell heredoc. The revision pins the weights and custom code. steps.title: Load the model and embed a sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForMaskedLM, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "MulinLab/hEVO-base-o"
# Freeze the checkpoint and its custom code for reproducible inference.
REVISION = "fa6139047c21d92b58bd8eda49ea2f89a884e33c"
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

load_options = dict(revision=REVISION, token=True, trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO, **load_options)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    use_frequency_embedding=False,
    use_flash_attention=False,
    **load_options,
)
assert config.use_frequency_embedding is False
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    REPO,
    config=config,
    attn_implementation="eager",
    dtype=torch.float32,
    **load_options,
).to(device).eval()

def encode_dna(sequence):
    sequence = sequence.strip().upper()
    if not 0 < len(sequence) <= config.max_position_embeddings:
        raise ValueError("Provide a sequence of 1 to 1,024 nucleotides.")
    if set(sequence) - set("ACGTN"):
        raise ValueError("DNA must contain only A, C, G, T or N.")
    encoded = tokenizer(sequence, return_tensors="pt", truncation=False)
    # This custom tokenizer returns 1D tensors for a single sequence.
    encoded = {
        key: value.unsqueeze(0) if value.ndim == 1 else value
        for key, value in encoded.items()
    }
    if "attention_mask" not in encoded:
        encoded["attention_mask"] = torch.ones_like(encoded["input_ids"])
    return {key: value.to(device) for key, value in encoded.items()}

sequence = "ACGTTGCATGTCGCATGATGCATGAGAGCT"
inputs = encode_dna(sequence)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(**inputs, output_hidden_states=True, return_dict=True)
    token_embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1]  # [batch, length, hidden_size]

    # Optional: summarize the last-layer nucleotide embeddings by mean pooling.
    keep = inputs["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1).to(token_embeddings.dtype)
    sequence_embedding = (token_embeddings * keep).sum(dim=1) / keep.sum(
        dim=1
    ).clamp_min(1)

print("Last-layer token embeddings:", tuple(token_embeddings.shape))
print("Mean-pooled sequence embedding:", tuple(sequence_embedding.shape))
EOF

profile.summary: hEVO-large-o is the larger of the two public checkpoints of hEvo, a DNA language model family from MulinLab trained on haplotype sequences from human populations. It reads a DNA sequence of up to 1,024 nucleotides and returns one 1,280-dimensional vector per nucleotide, plus masked-base predictions that can score a single-nucleotide variant as a log-likelihood ratio of the alternative against the reference allele. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: hEVO-large-o is a bidirectional BERT-style masked language model with 16 transformer layers and hidden size 1,280, and one token per nucleotide with no boundary tokens. The family README describes two training stages: span-masked representation learning on deduplicated haplotype windows, then calibration of the nucleotide prediction head on variant-centred contexts. To score a single-nucleotide variant, the variant site is masked once and the alternative-allele logit minus the reference-allele logit at that site gives the log-likelihood ratio. Frequency embeddings are disabled in this checkpoint's configuration, so inference uses DNA sequence only.

profile.summary: LncRFM is an RNA foundation model built for long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), whose function depends on both short sequence motifs and base pairing that can span thousands of nucleotides. It reads an RNA sequence and is pretrained to predict masked nucleotides, with masking guided by secondary structure; its encoder outputs can then be fine-tuned with a small task head for tasks such as lncRNA localisation, disease association or splice-site prediction. The authors also release the LncCorpus pretraining corpus and the LncBench benchmark.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LncRFM is a hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder. Its state-space kernels build on Mamba, and its bidirectional backbone follows the Hydra and HydraRNA design. The model code requires a motif stem, a motif gate and a pair-aware bidirectional mixer. The released configuration has 12 layers of width 768, motif convolution kernels of sizes 3 and 7, and attention layers with 12 heads at positions 5 and 11. It is pretrained by masked language modelling, using a structure-aware masking collator adapted from RNAErnie2 and training data that records each base's pairing partner. The pretraining launcher uses FP32, sequences of 200 to 2,048 nucleotides and 300,000 steps.

    **options,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    from_pretrained=str(checkpoint),
    dtype=torch.float32,
    device="cuda",
).eval()

inputs = tokenizer("[CLS] A U G [MASK] C [SEP]", return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")
with torch.no_grad():
